# Fixtures

The three CSVs in this directory (`transactions_stripe.csv`, `customers_saaS.csv`,
`events_product.csv`) are the canonical fixtures from `docs/decisions/01`, at 1,000 rows each.
They are **committed on purpose** — they are what proves the import pipeline's type inference and
timestamp handling, so do not "clean up" the odd-looking cells below. If a row here looks wrong,
that is the point; check `scripts/fixtures/*.ts` for the row index that put it there before
touching it.

All three are generated by `scripts/fixtures/generate.ts` from a seeded PRNG (mulberry32 — see
`scripts/fixtures/prng.ts`), never `Math.random()`. The same seed always produces byte-identical
output, on any machine — even in a different timezone — because every timestamp is formatted from
UTC getters (`scripts/fixtures/timestamps.ts`), never the host's local clock. This is not just
implemented that way, it is _tested_ that way: `scripts/fixtures/generate.test.ts`'s "timestamp
formatting is independent of the host machine's timezone" block fixes one instant, sets
`process.env.TZ` to `Pacific/Kiritimati` (UTC+14, deliberately as far from UTC as the IANA database
goes), and asserts the formatted string against a hardcoded expectation — a formatter that
regressed to local getters (`getHours()` instead of `getUTCHours()`) would print a different
wall-clock time there and fail. The determinism block above it does not exercise this: it builds
the same fixture twice in one process without ever changing `TZ`, so a local-getter formatter would
pass it too. The cross-timezone claim rests on the dedicated block, not on determinism alone.

Row indices below are **0-based data rows, header excluded** — "data row 3" is CSV line 5.

## Regenerating

```
npx tsx scripts/fixtures/generate.ts              # the three small fixtures above (default seed 42)
npx tsx scripts/fixtures/generate.ts --seed=123    # a different seed; every fixture changes
npx tsx scripts/fixtures/generate.ts --large       # also the 1,000,000-row variants, into generated/
npx tsx scripts/fixtures/generate.ts --wide        # also the 100-column variant, into generated/
```

`generated/` is gitignored — it holds only output that must never be committed (see below).

## Timestamp shapes (why they differ per fixture)

Per `docs/adr/0004`, naive (no-offset) timestamps are interpreted in the organization's timezone at
import time and stored as `timestamptz`; timestamps with an explicit offset keep their instant. The
three fixtures deliberately exercise different shapes so the import pipeline has to handle all of
them from one set of test data:

| Fixture               | Column(s)                   | Shape                                                                                      |
| --------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `transactions_stripe` | `created_at`                | ISO 8601 with a trailing `Z`, e.g. `2026-01-15T14:23:05Z` — always an instant, never naive |
| `customers_saaS`      | `created_at`, `canceled_at` | Naive local, e.g. `2026-01-15 14:23:05` — no offset, ever                                  |
| `events_product`      | `timestamp`                 | A **mix** of both shapes, chosen per row — the single hardest case: one column, two shapes |

## Dirty rows

Seven kinds of deliberately-dirty data appear across the three fixtures; each fixture carries the
ones its columns permit (`events_product` has no decimal column, so it skips the `N/A` /
`$1,234.56` cases; `transactions_stripe.created_at` always carries an offset, so it skips the DST
cases). All dirty rows sit at low, fixed indices (≤ 28) so they land inside type inference's
first-10,000-row sample per `docs/decisions/06` — including in the 1,000,000-row `--large` variant.
Two dirty decimal rows out of 1,000 still leaves 99.8% of sampled values parseable, comfortably
**above** the 95% inference threshold — so the column still infers as `decimal` despite the noise.
That combination (dirty, but not enough to flip inference) is exactly the property these fixtures
need: delete the `N/A` row and you've removed the thing that proves inference tolerates noise, not
just clean data.

### `transactions_stripe.csv`

| Data row | Column          | Value                              | Exercises                                                         |
| -------- | --------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 3        | `amount`        | `N/A`                              | unparseable decimal → `NULL` + `import_errors`                    |
| 7        | `amount`        | `$1,234.56`                        | currency-formatted decimal, not plain numeric                     |
| 11       | `customer_id`   | `0001234`                          | leading-zero identifier — must stay a string, never become `1234` |
| 15       | `plan_name`     | _(empty)_                          | empty cell → `NULL`, column nullable                              |
| 19       | `customer_name` | `Acme, "The Best" Co.` + a newline | comma + quote + newline in one field — CSV quoting round-trip     |

### `customers_saaS.csv`

| Data row | Column        | Value                            | Exercises                                                                                 |
| -------- | ------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 4        | `mrr`         | `N/A`                            | unparseable decimal                                                                       |
| 8        | `mrr`         | `$1,234.56`                      | currency-formatted decimal                                                                |
| 12       | `id`          | `0005678`                        | leading-zero identifier                                                                   |
| 16       | `canceled_at` | _(empty)_                        | empty cell on a nullable datetime column                                                  |
| 20       | `created_at`  | `2026-03-08 02:30:00`            | naive local time that **never occurred** — inside the America/New_York spring-forward gap |
| 24       | `canceled_at` | `2026-11-01 01:30:00`            | naive local time that occurred **twice** — inside the America/New_York fall-back overlap  |
| 28       | `name`        | `O, "Really" Big Co` + a newline | comma + quote + newline in one field                                                      |

### `events_product.csv`

| Data row | Column          | Value                                                                                                                                                                            | Exercises                                            |
| -------- | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| 5        | `session_id`    | _(empty)_                                                                                                                                                                        | empty cell on a nullable column                      |
| 9        | `user_id`       | `0009012`                                                                                                                                                                        | leading-zero identifier                              |
| 13       | `timestamp`     | `2026-03-08 02:30:00`                                                                                                                                                            | spring-forward gap, naive branch of the mixed column |
| 17       | `timestamp`     | `2026-11-01 01:30:00`                                                                                                                                                            | fall-back overlap, naive branch of the mixed column  |
| 21       | `metadata_json` | a JSON-shaped string with a comma, an escaped quote, and a newline (the embedded newline makes it not strictly valid JSON — that's deliberate, it's the CSV-quoting stress case) | comma + quote + newline in one field                 |

`events_product` has no decimal column, so it does not carry the `N/A` / `$1,234.56` cases.

## ⚠️ Ceiling conflict: "50 MB max" vs. "1,000,000 rows" (needs a decision in `docs/decisions/01`)

`docs/decisions/01` states two MVP ceilings side by side, as if a file could always be under both at
once: **"50 MB max per CSV"** and **"1,000,000 rows per dataset"** (§ "MVP Ceilings (Design
Targets)"). For these fixtures' schemas they are not simultaneously satisfiable — this is not a
generator shortcut, it is arithmetic, shown below. Do not "fix" this by quietly shrinking the
fixtures; the fixtures are honest about decision 01's own column/shape spec (ADR-0004's mandated
timestamp shapes, decision 01's fixture column lists). Shrinking them would hide the conflict, not
resolve it. This section exists so the Slice 1 performance spike (`docs/decisions/01` names it as
the place to "validate and adjust" these targets) has real numbers to decide from.

**Why 50 MB and 1,000,000 rows collide for this shape.** Each fixture's per-row size is fixed by its
columns: short synthetic IDs (`tx0000001`, `c000001`, …, not realistic Stripe-style tokens), and
timestamp columns that are 19–20 characters each because ADR-0004 mandates ISO-with-`Z` or
naive-local (`2026-01-15T14:23:05Z` / `2026-01-15 14:23:05`) — not a format anyone can shorten
without breaking the shape the import pipeline is meant to be tested against. `customers_saaS` and
`events_product` each carry _two_ datetime columns, which is why `customers_saaS` is the worst case
below.

**The arithmetic** (bytes ÷ rows = bytes/row). The committed 1,000-row file and the 1,000,000-row
`--large` variant of `transactions_stripe` and `events_product` agree to well under a percent
(78.456 vs. 78.513, 70.162 vs. 70.143), confirming bytes/row is a stable per-schema constant, not
sampling noise. `customers_saaS` diverges more (89.942 vs. 93.126, ~3.5%) because its
variable-length fields (company/plan names) are undersampled at only 1,000 rows; the 1,000,000-row
figure is the more reliable one and is what the table below uses:

| Fixture               | Bytes/row (1,000,000-row measurement) | Bytes at 1,000,000 rows  | Rows that fit in 50 MB |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| `transactions_stripe` | 78.513                                | 78,512,999 (**75.2 MB**) | ~667,772               |
| `customers_saaS`      | 93.126                                | 93,126,268 (**88.8 MB**) | ~562,986               |
| `events_product`      | 70.143                                | 70,143,452 (**66.9 MB**) | ~747,451               |

So for every one of the three canonical schemas, "50 MB" and "1,000,000 rows" name _different_
files: the 50 MB ceiling is hit between 563K and 748K rows, well before the row ceiling; the
1,000,000-row ceiling produces a file 34–78% over the byte ceiling. A CSV that is simultaneously
"1,000,000 rows" and "≤ 50 MB" does not exist for any of these three fixtures' column shapes, and
narrower synthetic fixtures than decision 01 already specifies would stop testing the real shape.

**Three ways to resolve it**, for whoever makes the call in `docs/decisions/01`:

1. **Raise the byte ceiling** — e.g. to ~100 MB, enough to cover `customers_saaS` (the worst case)
   at 1,000,000 rows with headroom for wider real-world columns.
2. **Lower the row ceiling** — e.g. to ~500,000 rows, so all three fixtures clear 50 MB at the full
   row count.
3. **Make the ceiling "whichever bound is hit first"** — stop treating "50 MB" and "1,000,000 rows"
   as a conjunction a real file must satisfy both of, and instead reject a file the moment it
   exceeds _either_ bound independently. A 200-column file hits 50 MB long before 1,000,000 rows; a
   6-column file hits 1,000,000 rows long before 50 MB. Both are legitimate MVP files under this
   reading; neither is under reading (1) or (2) alone.

**Recommendation: option 3.** It is the only one of the three that does not silently make some
already-planned fixture (or some real customer file) non-conformant by fiat — raising the byte cap
alone still cannot save a very wide 1,000,000-row file, and lowering the row cap alone still
under-serves a narrow file that could safely hold far more than 500K rows within 50 MB. It also
requires no change to either published number (50 MB, 1,000,000 rows) — only to how they combine —
and fits how `import.profile` already enforces ceilings "before any DDL" (`src/modules/imports/CLAUDE.md`):
a streaming byte-count check and a streaming row-count check are naturally two independent early
exits, not one combined formula, so option 3 is also the smallest implementation change.

Whichever option `docs/decisions/01` picks, **the benchmark gate must measure against the resolved
limit, not the two figures as currently written.** Concretely: decision 06's benchmark gate ("Profile
phase, 50 MB / 1M rows ≤ 90s"; "Load phase, 50 MB / 1M rows ≤ 5 min") currently names both figures
together as if one file could carry both — per the arithmetic above, for these schemas no such file
exists to benchmark. Once decision 01 resolves this (option 3: the actual ceiling a file can hit is
whichever bound — bytes or rows — it reaches first), the benchmark inputs should be the two _edge_
files that each hit exactly one bound: a ~1,000,000-row file at its natural byte size (this fixture
shape, unmodified) and a maximally-wide file sized to exactly 50 MB at well under 1,000,000 rows
(the `--wide` variant, extended) — not a single hypothetical file satisfying both numbers at once,
which the arithmetic above shows cannot exist.

The wide variant is `transactions_stripe`'s 9 columns plus 91 synthetic `metric_NN` columns to reach
exactly 100. It intentionally does **not** match decision 01's canonical column list, so it is never
committed and lives only in `generated/`.

## What's pure vs. what does I/O

`scripts/fixtures/{prng,csv,format,timestamps,pools,dirty,transactions,customers,events,wide}.ts`
are pure — no filesystem access, deterministic given a seed. `scripts/fixtures/generate.ts` is the
only file that touches disk; it is the CLI entry point and is not imported by
`scripts/fixtures/generate.test.ts`, which tests the pure modules directly.
